commit.message:
anny: bit-faithful HNSW graph serialization

Reopening a store used to mean re-inserting every vector: ~2,500
distance evaluations per node, tens of seconds at scale. The graph is
pure POD — vectors, fixed-width layer-0 adjacency rows, an upper-layer
arena, free lists, one xorshift state — so a snapshot can be a
header-validated bulk copy instead. write_to/read_from restore
bit-faithfully: searches AND subsequent inserts match the original
exactly, because free-list order and RNG state are captured. That is
stronger than the rebuild path, whose fjall-key-order reinsertion
produces a different-but-equivalent graph.

NodeMeta has padding, so it is serialized as parallel arrays (level,
upper, alive) and never written as the raw struct. Header mismatches
(DIM, M0, MAX_LEVEL, dtype width) are rejected as InvalidData, and
every unchecked-indexed structure is shape-validated on read.

commit.message:
fold: load the Hnsw sink from a graph snapshot when one is valid

init now tries the file named by with_graph_snapshot(path) before
falling back to the re-insert rebuild. A snapshot loads only when it
matches committed rows exactly — every row key present in the blob's
id map, counts equal — and anything else (missing file, truncation, a
stale blob left behind by later commits) silently rebuilds. This
matters because the blob carries no payload checksum: agreement with
the rows is the integrity check.

HnswReader::save_graph writes through with_state, so a graph marked
stale by an aborted transaction resyncs from committed rows before it
is captured. The write is tmp-then-rename atomic.

Measured in the seance example: reopening a cloned store drops from
~1.5s (rebuild-bound) to tens of milliseconds.

commit.message:
fold: bounded journals and a maintenance handle on the store

Two levers that directory-snapshot checkpointing needs.

Stream::new caps max_journaling_size at fjall's 64MiB floor. Opening a
store — or a copied snapshot of its directory — replays the journal,
and the 512MiB default let one mega-transaction cost ~1s of replay on
every open (139MB measured). The cap bounds that replay debt.

Stream::db() and KeyedStream::db() expose the underlying database for
maintenance the pipeline model cannot express: memtable rotation
before snapshotting a directory, and periodic major_compact of
posting-heavy keyspaces. Without the latter, Bm25 query latency grows
~50x per 1,000 commits of churn from LSM read amplification; a
compact every 200 commits holds it flat. Writes through this handle
would desynchronize the sinks, and the doc says so.

fold/examples/fjall_clone_probe.rs is the empirical basis for
snapshots: clone a live db dir, open the clone, diverge both, verify
isolation and per-inode lock behavior.

commit.message:
seance: time-travel search over any git repository

A repo's history becomes a delta stream: each commit's diff is upserts
and removals on a KeyedStream<path, Doc>, and fold maintains seven
views through it — Bm25 postings, an ese-embedded HNSW graph, a
document table, counts, per-extension aggregates, line stats, and a
temporal chronicle. Moving the cursor applies one diff, forward or
backward; retraction is what makes backward identical to forward, and
the probe (--probe) proves it: HEAD -> first -> HEAD leaves every
deterministic view byte-identical.

The latency architecture, in layers:

- Walks: jumps of <=300 commits step one commit per transaction
  (~20ms), streaming a searchable view of every intermediate state.
  Per-step diffs come from one batched git log per range; blob sizes
  gate transport through cat-file --batch-check so megablobs never
  cross a pipe.
- Chronicle: a KeyedRanked temporal index over ALL history (path ->
  Scored<birth_commit, blob-oid>; git is the content store). Built
  once in the background (23,525 commits in ~11s, 16MB), it answers
  stats and file versions as-of any commit in 1-3us with zero writes.
- Checkpoints: dwell in an era for 500ms and the live store is fsynced
  and CoW-cloned (~40ms inline) into an immutable master, then washed
  in the background. A return visit clones the master and opens it in
  tens of milliseconds — including the vector graph, via the anny
  snapshot. Warp end-to-end: 61ms.

Lessons paid for in benchmarks, kept as comments at the sites:

- Bm25's set-semantic flush corrupts term frequencies if one
  transaction retracts and re-inserts the same document; goto uses a
  retract transaction, then bounded insert chunks (which also keep
  journal replay bounded for the snapshot path).
- Embeddings are computed outside the pipeline in one rayon batch and
  stored in the record, so retraction never re-embeds.
- The wash rebuilds masters into born-fresh stores and never deletes
  journal files: fjall's active journal is a bare-numbered
  preallocated file, sealed ones are N.jnl, and hand-deleting either
  corrupts descendants one generation later. Ballast writes past the
  hardcoded 64MB rotation threshold let fjall's own eviction collect
  the fat journals; promotion is gated by a warp rehearsal (clone the
  master, open the clone).
- Interrupted teleports abandon at read-only phase boundaries, so a
  drag cancels stale multi-second jumps in ~20-150ms without writing.

commit.message:
seance: benchmark harness against sqlite fts5 and git grep

One workload, three contenders: materialize sqlite.git at HEAD-2000,
apply commits forward one at a time, run the same queries after every
step, same content rules everywhere, same ese vectors handed to the
baseline (--dump-vecs). Machine-readable JSONL on stdout from all
three; bench.py summary/capsummary render the tables in RESULTS.md.

Headlines: semantic top-10 68us vs 43.3ms flat scan (637x,
sub-linear vs O(n)); hybrid keyword+semantic+rrf 359us vs 43.4ms
(121x); keyword parity with FTS5 (0.3 vs 0.2ms); stats <1us vs 60us.
Honest losses, disclosed with causes: FTS5 wins raw apply 10x (one
index vs seven views plus embeddings), cold jumps 5.5x, and single-file
snapshots (10ms — genuinely good). The report states every bias,
and the two biases in the semantic comparison run against bog.

The harness earned its keep: it discovered the churn-driven Bm25
query degradation and measured the compaction cadence that fixes it.

commit.message:
seance: strip submission scaffolding from the tree

The PR body carries the submission template, so the tracked copy is
redundant; the editor backup of RESULTS.md never belonged in the tree
at all. Cargo.lock is regenerated without the ouija package entry — a
local-only scaffold that leaked into the lock because cargo resolves
every examples/* member it can see, tracked or not. Checkouts of this
branch now build --locked without a phantom member.
